trap.wrong: "They're inside our private network, so internal calls are trusted."
trap.why: Network location isn't identity. One compromised service or misconfigured route gives an attacker access to everything internal. Zero trust assumes the network is hostile.
trap.probe: Workload identity, mTLS, per-call authorisation, and propagating end-user context.
trap.say: "Every workload gets a cryptographic identity (mTLS certificates from SPIFFE or the mesh), services authorise which callers may call which endpoints, and end-user context travels as a signed token so downstream services can enforce user-level permissions."

thesis: Internal calls need real authentication and authorisation: each workload has a short-lived cryptographic identity, connections use mutual TLS, services authorise callers per endpoint, and end-user identity is propagated in signed tokens rather than trusted headers.
pitch: I'd give every service a workload identity issued automatically, such as a SPIFFE id via SPIRE or the service mesh's certificate authority, with short-lived certificates rotated automatically, so there are no long-lived shared secrets. Connections use mTLS, so both sides prove who they are and traffic is encrypted. Then authorisation: the payments service accepts calls to 'create payout' only from the disbursement service, expressed as policy in the mesh or in the service. Third, user context: when a request originates from a user, the edge validates their token and passes a signed, short-lived internal token or the original token downstream, so a service can check 'may this user do this', not just 'may this service call me'. Plain headers like X-User-Id are forgeable by any compromised service. I'd also log caller identity on every call for audit, and keep a break-glass path for operations.

points.d: Each service instance gets an identity bound to what it is (service, environment), issued and rotated automatically.
Both client and server present certificates; traffic is encrypted and authenticated. A service mesh can do this transparently.
Allow-lists of which services may call which endpoints or methods, enforced at the mesh or in the service.
Signed tokens carrying user identity and scopes, verified downstream; never trust bare identity headers.
API keys shared among services leak and are hard to rotate; short-lived certificates or tokens avoid that.
Log which workload and which user initiated each sensitive call.

decision: mTLS with automatically issued workload identities everywhere, service-level allow-lists for sensitive endpoints, and signed user-context tokens for user-initiated calls.
numbers: Certificate lifetimes of hours (rather than years) limit the usefulness of a stolen certificate; rotation must therefore be fully automated.
pitfalls: Trusting anything from inside the VPC.
Shared API keys between services checked into config.
mTLS enabled but no authorisation, so any internal service can call anything.

followups.q: How do you migrate an existing fleet to mTLS?
followups.a: Deploy the mesh or sidecars in permissive mode (accept both), observe traffic and identities, then switch services to strict mode one by one.
The same workload identity system, with identities for jobs and narrow permissions, not a shared admin credential.
Swapping an incoming user token for a downstream token scoped to the next service (RFC 8693), limiting what each hop can do.

example: After an SSRF bug let an attacker call internal admin endpoints, a company rolled out a service mesh with SPIFFE identities and strict mTLS, plus per-endpoint allow-lists. The same bug class would now be rejected because the vulnerable service isn't authorised to call admin APIs.
